scenes.headline: Why ube is everywhere
scenes.sub: The purple yam behind your favourite desserts
scenes.purpose: Hook: name the obsession and promise the why.
scenes.voiceover: Ube cake, ube ice cream, ube pandesal. In the Philippines, this purple root is everywhere. So what makes it so special?

scenes.headline: It's a yam, not taro
scenes.sub: Ube is Dioscorea alata, the purple yam
scenes.purpose: Clear up the most common mix-up.
scenes.voiceover: First, ube is not taro. It's a yam, Dioscorea alata, with a sweeter, nuttier taste and a deep violet flesh.

scenes.headline: The purple is natural
scenes.sub: The same pigments that colour blueberries
scenes.purpose: Explain the colour that makes it famous.
scenes.voiceover: That colour isn't dye. Ube is rich in anthocyanins, the same natural pigments you find in blueberries and red cabbage.

scenes.headline: of stirring for real halaya
scenes.sub: Grated ube, milk, butter and sugar over low heat
scenes.purpose: A concrete number that shows the craft.
scenes.voiceover: Ube halaya, the classic jam, takes patience. Grated ube, milk, butter and sugar, stirred over low heat for up to an hour.

scenes.headline: Halo-halo means mix-mix
scenes.sub: Ube halaya often crowns the top
scenes.purpose: Tie ube to the most iconic Filipino dessert.
scenes.voiceover: And then there's halo-halo, literally mix-mix. Shaved ice, beans, fruit, leche flan, and very often a scoop of ube on top.

scenes.headline: Now the world wants it
scenes.sub: Ube flavours show up in bakeries far from home
scenes.purpose: Widen out: from local staple to global trend.
scenes.voiceover: Today you'll find ube lattes and ube donuts in cities all over the world, carried by Filipino bakers and a very photogenic colour.

scenes.headline: Taste the purple
scenes.voiceover: Sweet, nutty, and unmistakably purple. Next merienda, make it ube.
